$comment: SERVICE BUS QUEUE AND ROLE REGISTRY. What the trigger contract could not say.
specs/001-platform-scaffold/contracts/triggers.md defines the MESSAGES — their kinds, their
closed field sets, what they do and do not carry, and the consumer's obligations. It cannot say
which queues exist, what their transport settings are, or which identity may send on which one.
Until this file existed those lived only in role scopes inside managed-identities.json, which
named queues nothing declared.
A QUEUE THAT EXISTS ONLY IN A ROLE SCOPE IS A QUEUE NOBODY PROVISIONS. The role assignment
deploys cleanly against a namespace with no such queue, the publisher then fails at first use,
and the failure names an authorization problem rather than a missing resource.
THE TRANSPORT SETTINGS ARE PART OF THE CONTRACT, not tuning. `maxDeliveryCount`, the lock
duration and the message time-to-live are what make 'an expired message dead-letters rather
than executing' true — stated in triggers.md as a rule and configured here as the mechanism.
Changing one without the other makes the document describe a system that does not exist.
$separation: THREE QUEUES, NOT ONE, AND THE SEPARATION IS A TRIAGE CONTROL (triggers.md).
synthia-triggers carries the resume trigger. The two integration queues carry the execution
seam. Mixing them would make dead-letter triage ambiguous: an operator finding a dead-lettered
message could not tell 'approved work never ran' from 'a result never returned', and those call
for different actions — the first is a governance failure that surfaces in the
approved-but-not-executed list, the second is an operational one.
COMMANDS AND RESULTS ARE ALSO SEPARATE FROM EACH OTHER, for the same reason one level down.
They flow in opposite directions between different principals, so one queue would mean each
service held both send and listen on it — and 'RagCore cannot publish a result' would stop
being enforceable by role assignment at all.

queues.name: synthia-triggers
queues.purpose: Approval, consent and sample-flow triggers. RagCore publishes; RagCore's workers consume.
$comment: Pre-existing. Listed here so the registry is the whole picture rather than the new half —
a file describing two of three queues is one a reader trusts for the wrong set.
ORDERING IS NOT ASSUMED ANYWHERE (triggers.md), so sessions are off. Enabling them would
impose an ordering guarantee no consumer relies on, at the cost of head-of-line blocking:
one poison message would stall every message sharing its session.

queues.name: synthia-integration-commands
queues.purpose: RagCore asks the Integrations Service to execute an authorized capability.
$comment: THE MESSAGE CARRIES jobId, correlationId AND kind, AND NOTHING ELSE (FR-INTEG-014). The
organisation, the capability, its version, its parameters and the authority all come from
the durable integration_job row the identifier names. A field the contract does not name is
refused and dead-lettered rather than sanitised.
messageTimeToLive MATCHES THE EXECUTION WINDOW, and that is the point rather than a
coincidence. A command outliving the authority that permitted it must dead-letter rather
than execute; expiry at the transport is what makes that true even if every consumer is
down. The consumer re-checks the window against durable state as well — two mechanisms,
because the transport cannot see an approval that was revoked inside the window.
lockDuration is longer than any single connector call's timeout, so a slow external system
cannot cause redelivery WHILE THE FIRST ATTEMPT IS STILL RUNNING. That specific race is how
an at-least-once queue produces two external effects from one authorization — and the
derived idempotency key is the second line of defence against it, not the first.
A DEAD-LETTERED COMMAND IS A GOVERNANCE FAILURE, not an operational one: it means approved
work never ran. It surfaces in the approved-but-not-executed list with an alert, and
recovery is fresh authorization — NEVER replay (FR-EXEC-006).

queues.name: synthia-integration-results
queues.purpose: The Integrations Service reports an execution outcome back to RagCore.
$comment: The result message carries the same three fields. RagCore reads the outcome from the four
result columns on its own integration_job row, not from the message — so a lost or
duplicated result cannot change what the platform believes happened.
AN `integration.failed` IS NEVER A RE-DISPATCH (FR-INTEG-027). It is consumed, recorded and
escalated. A consumer that re-published a command on failure would spend one authority
record repeatedly, which is the loop the no-retry rule exists to prevent.
A dead-lettered RESULT is operational rather than governance: the effect may well have
happened, and what is lost is RagCore's knowledge of it. The execution record in the
Integrations Service's schema is the reconciliation source — which is why the result columns
carry the execution id.

roleAssignments.why: RagCore dispatches authorized work. Send only: it must not be able to consume its own commands.
RagCore consumes outcomes and resumes the graph. Receive only: it must not be able to publish a result.
The Integrations Service consumes commands. Receive only: it must not be able to dispatch work to itself.
It publishes the outcome through its own transactional outbox. Send only.

$leastPrivilege: FOUR ASSIGNMENTS, EACH ONE DIRECTION ON ONE QUEUE. Neither service holds both roles on either
integration queue, and that asymmetry is the control rather than tidiness:
- RagCore cannot publish an `integration.completed`. If it could, a compromised orchestrator
could fabricate a successful outcome for work that never ran — and because RagCore reads
the outcome from its own row rather than the message, the forgery would have to be paired
with a database write it also cannot make (migration 0022 grants it no UPDATE on the result
- The Integrations Service cannot dispatch work to itself. Every execution it performs traces
to a command RagCore published against a job row RagCore wrote.
DATA OWNER IS DELIBERATELY NOT USED ANYWHERE. It would collapse each pair into one line and
additionally grant management of queues and subscriptions, which no runtime component does.
SCOPED TO THE QUEUE, NEVER THE NAMESPACE. A namespace-scoped Sender would let either service
publish to synthia-triggers and forge an approval trigger, which is the one message class that
moves work past a human decision.
